opening_summary: Thirty-four terms for game art, from what makes a picture clear, to how concept art narrows ideas, to how a sculpt becomes a model the engine can run. Exact terms turn a vague art request into one you can check.
opening_description: 34 art terms: clarity, concept and character art.

idea.narration: Hallo. This is Liam, in for Bear. Newcomers often say concept art is the finished art of a game. It is not. Concept art is early, rough drawing that solves a design problem for the team, and its polish hardly matters. Game art is full of look-alike terms like that. This film goes through them group by group, each one shown, so you can name the exact one.
idea.text:
Concept art is
the finished game art.
idea.replacementWords: a rough sketch that solves a problem

beats.narration: This table is the map. Thirty-four art terms in four groups. The first group is what art must do, with clarity, satisfaction, art style and pushed proportions. These are the jobs game art has, and the look it sets.

The second group is steering the eye. Visual hierarchy, contrast and its kinds, light and dark, colour, shape and size, then silhouette, shape language, area of focus, rest and high detail, and atmospheric perspective. These decide what a player sees first.

The third group is concept art. Concept art itself, reference, mood board, the constraint and its three kinds, thematic, perspective and mechanics, then ideation, two-tone sketching, closing doors and iteration. These are how early designs are found and narrowed.

The fourth group is character art. Iconic elements, proxy model, readability, high-poly sculpt, low-poly mesh, UV map and unwrapping, texture baking, anatomy and neutral pose. These take a design all the way to a character in the game.

Eight things drawn at game size. Clarity means the player can tell at once what is happening, who is friend or foe, and where to go. In this made-up example a thing counts as readable at sixteen pixels or more and three to one contrast, and only four of the eight pass. For example, a spike trap drawn in the same brown as the floor fails clarity, because the player sees the danger only after landing on it.

Satisfaction means each action gets a quick, responsive answer, so acting feels good. Both squares answer the same press. In this made-up example the fast one answers in forty milliseconds, and the slow one in seven hundred, six hundred sixty later, and it lags. Clarity asks whether you can tell what is going on. Satisfaction asks whether it feels good to act. For example, a coin that pops and chimes the instant the player touches it is satisfying.

Art style is the consistent look of a game, its colour, its designs and its shapes. These two pictures share the same shapes and layout. Only the colour use differs, a mean saturation of zero point eight one against zero point one one, and the scene feels quite different. For example, if your game is flat pixel art in a small, bright palette, every new enemy and coin must follow that choice, or it looks out of place.

Pushed proportions are shapes exaggerated on purpose, as in a cartoon look. The three figures share one body, and the red head grows from fourteen percent of the height, about realistic, to twenty-two, then thirty-three. For example, a player character drawn with an oversized head and short legs reads as a cartoon on purpose, not as a realistic person.

Six circles, and a bar for each. Visual hierarchy means arranging a picture so the most important things are seen first, then the next, in order. Here attention is scored as size times contrast, a simple stand-in. The boss gets forty-six percent, the player twenty-two, the rock only three. Contrast is one difference, and hierarchy is the order the eye visits. For example, on a title menu the Start button should be seen first, the options next, and the credits last.

Contrast is any difference that pulls the eye to one place, and it can be measured. Three colour pairs sit on a scale from one to twenty-one. White on cream is one point one one to one, almost invisible. Dark ink on cream is eleven point two three to one, and black on white is twenty-one to one. For example, a white score number on a pale sky is hard to see, and a dark outline around it raises its contrast.

Light and dark contrast is the gap between light and dark areas, with hue taken away. Each colour on top is shown below as its grey. Red and blue look very different, yet both land at zero point one three, almost the same grey. Light and dark contrast survives a black and white copy, and colour alone often does not. For example, turn a level screenshot grey. If a red enemy and a blue floor become one grey, make the enemy much lighter or darker.

Colour contrast means strong differences in colour or saturation, how pure a colour is. In each row one circle is the odd one. In the top row its saturation is zero point seven six among circles at zero point zero seven, and it jumps out. In the bottom row the gap is only zero point one three, and it hides. For example, one bright gold key in a grey stone room is found at once.

Two rows of seven shapes. Shape and size contrast means one thing differs in size or outline from the rest, so it is seen first, or it points the way. In the top row one circle is twice the median size. In the bottom row one shape has three corners, and the other six have none. For example, an exit door far taller than the small crates around it is spotted the moment the player enters the room.

Silhouette is the outline of an object alone, and it should still say what the object is when filled black at game size. A knight and a blob are filled black and shrunk from forty-eight down to six. The tell-apart score is one minus their overlap, and it stays between zero point four two and zero point five three at every size. For example, fill a new enemy sprite black beside the player, at its size in the level, and check you can still name it.

Now the knight sits beside a near copy, the same outline with small differences. At forty-eight the tell-apart score is only zero point zero six, and by six it is zero. The two outlines have become one. Small details vanish as a silhouette shrinks. For example, two enemies that differ only by a belt buckle look like the same enemy at game size, so give one of them a different overall outline.

Shape language is how the forms of a design express its personality or idea. Three forms are measured by their sharpest corner. Rounded at one hundred sixty-five degrees, blocky at ninety, spiky at twenty-five. The number only describes the form, and what it says is the artist's choice. Shape and size contrast is about standing out. Shape language is about meaning. For example, you give a friendly shopkeeper soft, round shapes and a boss sharp spikes, and keep that rule across the whole game.

A checkerboard with one black square in the middle. Area of focus is the place in an image where the artist wants the eye to land. The centre against its neighbour is seven point nine to one. The outer neighbours are only two point four to one, so the eye goes to the centre. For example, on the last screen of a level, the exit door can be the area of focus, the one spot the art steers the player toward.

Rest and high detail means leaving plain regions beside a busy one, so the busy part reads as important. In this made-up example both rows spend the same sixty-four strokes. Spread evenly, the focus tile holds thirteen percent. Concentrated, with rest around it, it holds sixty-seven percent. Area of focus is where the eye should land, and rest is what makes it land there. For example, keep a level's floor tiles plain and spend the detail on the one carved door the player must find.

Atmospheric perspective means faraway things lose detail and contrast, which adds depth and guides the eye. Six trees stand farther and farther to the right. With a made-up falloff, their contrast drops from one hundred percent to seventeen, and their detail lines thin out. For example, in a side-scrolling level you paint the far mountains pale and plain and the near trees dark and detailed, so the player knows what is only background.

A scatter of forty sketches. Concept art is early drawing that solves a design problem for the team, not finished art. In this simulated set the red dots solve three or four of four problems, fifteen of the forty. Polish tells you almost nothing, a correlation of zero point zero one. For example, a page of rough sketches that each try a different way to show where a jumping enemy will land is concept art, even if none is clean.

Reference means real-world images and examples gathered to research a subject before drawing. Here, in this simulated set, twenty-four images are gathered, three groups of eight from different places. Reference is any image you gather. A mood board is a chosen set that shows the tone. For example, before drawing a termite enemy you collect photos of real termites, their jaws, their legs and the way they stand, and you note where each photo came from.

A mood board is a set of reference images that shows the theme and tone, shown to the team early. From the same twenty-four, two boards of six are chosen. The ink dots are a narrow board with a spread of thirty-one pixels. The red rings are scattered, two hundred eighteen, about seven times wider. The narrow one points the team one way. For example, six pictures of dim, wet caves pinned together set the tone for an underground level.

Sixty dots stand for sixty ideas, in this simulated set. A constraint is a limit that narrows what the artist designs. With no limit all sixty stay open, and nothing says which way to go. A constraint narrows the design, and reference is images gathered for research. For example, telling the agent that a new enemy may use only the few palette colours the player uses is a constraint on its design.

A thematic constraint is a limit that comes from the game's lore, setting and tone. Here the thematic limit turns twenty-nine ideas hollow, ideas that do not fit the world, and thirty-one stay open. For example, a game set inside an underground termite colony rules out shiny robots and spaceships, however good they look.

A perspective constraint is a limit that comes from the player's view, first person, third person or top down. The view limit shuts thirteen more ideas, and eighteen stay open. For example, Walker is seen from the side, so the termite reference, which shows the creatures from above, may not fit a side-view level without a new drawing.

A mechanics constraint is a limit that comes from the game's rules and numbers, such as an ability or a health total. The rules limit shuts seven more, and eleven of the sixty ideas are left. For example, if an enemy is defeated when the player jumps on its head, its design needs a clear top the player can see and land on.

Twenty-four rough thumbnails. Ideation means making many quick, rough ideas before choosing one. Drawing fast and loose gets the idea across without polish. In this made-up example each sketch takes about five seconds, so all twenty-four take one hundred twenty seconds. For example, before asking for a final coin sprite, you fill a page with quick coin shapes, stars, gems and rings, and only then pick one.

Two-tone sketching means sketching in only two colours, so you cannot fuss over small detail. In full colour this picture has eleven colours to decide. In two tones it has two, and only the big shapes stay in view. For example, block out a new level's background in just dark and light first, and add colour only once the big shapes work.

Closing doors means each round shuts the options that failed, and they are not reopened. Each row is one round. Twenty-four ideas become twelve, then six, then three, keeping the better half each time. Closing doors drops whole options, and iteration reworks the one that is kept. For example, once the team drops the flying version of an enemy, nobody brings it back at the next review.

Iteration means repeating a cycle of draft, feedback and change. The line is the gap to what the team needs. In this simulated run it shrinks from one point zero zero to zero point zero four over five cycles. Show work early, not in one grand reveal. For example, you show a rough jump animation to a playtester, hear that the landing feels stiff, change it, and show it again.

Seven features of one character, ranked. Iconic elements are the few features that keep a character recognisable even when tiny on screen. In this made-up example a feature shows only if its thinnest side is at least three pixels. The pauldron, the shoulder armour, survives down to twenty-seven pixels, the sword and scarf to thirty-two, the buckle needs ninety-six. For example, if your hero is known by a red scarf, draw the scarf big enough to show when the hero is small, and let tiny buckles go.

A proxy model is a rough block model of the big shapes, used to check proportions and silhouette early. The black blocks are the proxy, and the dashed red outline is the target. Over three rounds of correction the size error falls from nineteen percent to two. For example, before anyone sculpts a new enemy in Blender, you stack three boxes for its head, body and legs and check its height beside the player in Godot.

Readability is how well a character can be understood in the game's real view. One character is drawn at three sizes. At two hundred pixels all seven features show. At sixty-four, six of seven. At thirty-two, only three. Silhouette is the outline alone, and readability is the whole character at its real size. For example, judge a new enemy sprite in the running game, next to the player, not zoomed in inside an image viewer.

A circle, the outline of a very smooth sphere. A high-poly sculpt is a very detailed model, shaped like clay, holding all the detail and far too heavy for the engine. This sphere has one million forty-six thousand five hundred twenty-eight triangles, more than a game can draw in real time. For example, a character sculpted in Blender with every wrinkle and scale in its mesh is a high-poly sculpt, and it stays in Blender.

A low-poly mesh is a simplified copy of the sculpt with far fewer polygons, light enough for the engine to run. The red sphere has sixteen sides and two hundred twenty-four triangles, four thousand six hundred seventy-two times fewer. Its edge is off by one point nine percent, so the silhouette holds, but the detail is gone. For example, the model you export from Blender into Godot is the low-poly mesh, not the sculpt.

A UV map, named for the two axes of a flat image, is the flat layout of a model's surface used to place a texture. Unwrapping is the cutting that makes it. A cube has six faces and twelve edges. Cut seven, the red dashes, keep five joined, and it lies flat as a cross, each face with a place to paint. For example, in Blender you mark seams down the back of a character's coat, unwrap it, and paint the coat on the flat image.

Texture baking stores the sculpt's detail as an image on the low-poly mesh. The top row is how light shades the bumpy high-poly surface. The flat low-poly misses the bumps, off by zero point three seven. With the baked image it is off by only zero point zero four. For example, you bake the wrinkles of a high-poly boot into a normal map, so the low-poly boot in Godot still looks wrinkled.

A two-bone arm reaches for six targets from a shoulder on the left. Anatomy means knowing how bones and muscles work, so a sculpt looks believable and can be animated. The jointed limb, with an elbow, reaches five of the six targets. A rigid bar of the same length reaches one. The grey target is out of range. For example, give a spider enemy knee joints in the right places, and its walk animation can bend each leg naturally.

The neutral pose is the default pose a model is built in, and some designs that look right in it fail once the character moves. Each arm is raised from that pose until a shoulder plate blocks it. The heavy plate stops it at ninety-six degrees, and the trimmed plate at one hundred seven. Anatomy is how the body works, the neutral pose is how it stands while built. For example, a knight with huge shoulder armour may look fine standing, then cannot raise its sword overhead to attack.

Each pair sets two look-alike terms side by side. Contrast is a difference between two things, like this pair at eleven point two to one. Visual hierarchy is the order in which many things are seen, first, second, third and fourth.
Reference is any image gathered for research, here twelve, spread over one hundred ten pixels. A mood board is a narrow chosen set that sets the tone, here five images, tight and on theme.

A proxy model is rough blocks to check proportions, three blocks, size only. A low-poly mesh is the light copy of a sculpt that the engine runs, sixteen sides and two hundred twenty-four triangles. The proxy comes before the sculpt, the low-poly after it.

Silhouette is the outline alone, filled black, here twenty-four by twenty-four. Readability is whether the character is understood in the game's real view. As it shrinks, seven of seven features show, then six, then three.

A vague request sits above the exact instruction that replaces it, beside a chart of what it does. Make the enemy pop becomes, raise the enemy against the floor from one point two to one, to at least three to one. Four point two to one passes.

Make the hero readable becomes, fill the silhouette black at twenty-four pixels and keep its tell-apart score from the enemy above zero point three zero. Against the blob it scores zero point four four. The near copy, at zero point zero six, fails.

Draw the eye to the hero becomes, put at least sixty percent of the detail budget on the focal tile. Forty-three of sixty-four is sixty-seven percent. Spread evenly it is thirteen percent, and only the concentrated tile passes.

The mood is all over the place becomes, choose six images within sixty pixels of their centre. The narrow board spreads thirty-one pixels and passes. The scattered set spreads two hundred eighteen and does not.
I cannot pick one idea becomes, drop the weaker half each round, twenty-four, twelve, six, three, and never reopen a door once it is closed. Twenty-four ideas become three in three rounds.

This is a checklist of six questions to ask before you call a piece of art ready. First, can a player tell what is happening at once, and does the game answer each action? That is clarity, then satisfaction.
Second, where does the eye land first, and is that the most important thing on screen? That is visual hierarchy, and the area of focus.
Third, fill the silhouette black at the size it has in the game. Does the shape still say what it is, and can it be told apart from its neighbours?
Fourth, which constraint does this design solve, and what reference is it built on? Concept art exists to solve a problem, so name the problem.
Fifth, did you show the work early, and ask a specific question about the goal? That is iteration, not a grand reveal at the end.
Sixth, does the character hold up at the size it has in the game's real view? That is readability. Then say it exactly, a number, a size, a limit, not make it better.

recap_lines: Clarity is telling what is going on, and satisfaction is feeling good to act.
Contrast is one difference, and visual hierarchy is the order the eye visits.
A silhouette must still say what it is, filled black at game size.
Concept art solves a design problem, and its polish hardly matters.
Constraints narrow the ideas, and closing doors drops the weaker ones each round.
A high-poly sculpt's detail is baked onto the low-poly mesh the engine runs.

your_turn.segment: Name The Art Term, Defend It
your_turn.command: Quiz me on game art terms with short game-making cases, one at a time. Use the terms clarity, satisfaction, visual hierarchy, contrast, silhouette, readability, reference, mood board, proxy model and low-poly mesh. For each case I must name the exact term and say why its look-alike is wrong. Hold back the answer until I reply, then tell me if I was right.
checks: Check: each case is a game-making situation, and the answer waits for you.
Check: you named the exact term and said why its look-alike is wrong.

deck_problems: Slide 2 (Clarity, satisfaction and style), step 2: the caption starts a sentence in lower case after a full stop: 'the game answers the press at once. a 40 ms answer feels immediate'.

Slide 3 step 2: the printed luminances do not reproduce the printed ratio. With 'L 0.03 and 0.90' the formula (0.90 + 0.05) / (0.03 + 0.05) gives 11.88 : 1, not 11.23 : 1; the dark L must be about 0.035 before rounding. Print three decimals or say the L values are rounded. The caption also says 'from Chapter 6' on screen.
Slide 3 step 4: 'odd 0.76 vs others 0.07, gap 0.68', but 0.76 minus 0.07 is 0.69 as printed (rounding of unrounded values).

Slide 4 step 2: the knight-and-blob tell-apart score is not monotonic (0.45, 0.44, 0.42, then 0.53 at the smallest size), and the 6 x 6 cell panel shown as the headline is the size where the knight is least recognisable. The size axis (48, 24, 12, 6) has no unit.

Slide 5 step 1: the heading says the outer squares fade, but renderFocus lowers the contrast of every square except the centre by the same amount, so the board fades evenly, not toward the edges; 'two outer neighbours' means any two neighbouring non-centre squares.

Badges claim more than the notes: slide 5 and slide 9 are badged Computed, but the notes say the detail counts and the 0.35 falloff (slide 5), and the feature sizes and the 3 px rule (slide 9), are illustrative or invented. The narration calls those numbers made up.
Slide 9 step 3: the caption says unreadable features are 'Dashed red', but at 64 px and 32 px they show only as small red specks, not visibly dashed.

Slide 11 step 1: the caption names 'the rigid bar (dashed)', but at the end of the step the arm is fully stretched along the same line and covers the dashed bar, so the bar is not visible in the final picture. The second caption line ('Red rings: within reach ...') also crowds the TELL THESE APART heading below it.
Slide 12 step 2: the mood board is '5 chosen', while slides 6 and 13 use boards of six images; and only about four of the five dots can be told apart because they overlap.
Slide 13 step 1: the notes say the numbers are taken from earlier slides, but 1.2 : 1 and 4.2 : 1 appear on no earlier slide.
Slide 13 step 2: the dashed 0.30 threshold line runs through the labels 'vs enemy blob 0.44' and 'vs near copy 0.06'.
Slide 8 is badged Simulation (seeded), while step 1 rests on an assumed figure (5 seconds per sketch); the step says so, but the badge does not.
